body.text: Global supply chains and geopolitical balances increasingly pivot around Indira Gandhi. Tracking the primary facts helps separate durable structural shifts from daily noise.

Indira Priyadarshini Gandhi (née Nehru, 19 November 1917, 31 October 1984) was an Indian stateswoman who twice served as the Prime Minister of India from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until her assassination in 1984.

She was India's first and only female prime minister, and a central figure in Indian politics as the leader of the Indian National Congress (INC). Gandhi also served as chairperson of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) from 1983 to 1984, becoming the first Indian to hold the position.
She was the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister of India, and the mother of Rajiv Gandhi, who succeeded her as prime minister.

Gandhi was married to Feroze Gandhi, a Member of Parliament, with whom she had two sons, Rajiv Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi. During her father Jawaharlal Nehru's premiership from 1947 to 1964, Gandhi was his hostess and accompanied him on his numerous foreign trips.

In 1959, she played a part in the dissolution of the communist-led Kerala state government as then-president of the Indian National Congress, otherwise a ceremonial position to which she was elected earlier that year.

Lal Bahadur Shastri, who had succeeded Nehru as prime minister upon his death in 1964, appointed her minister of information and broadcasting in his government, the same year she was elected to the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of the Indian Parliament, representing Uttar Pradesh.

After Shastri's death in January 1966, Gandhi defeated Morarji Desai in the INC's parliamentary leadership election to become leader and succeeded Shastri as prime minister. With her premiership of India she became the world's second female prime minister after Sri Lanka's Sirimavo Bandaranaike.

She led the Congress to a majority in the 1967 Indian general election, in which she was first elected to the lower house of the Indian parliament, the Lok Sabha, from Rae Bareli, in Uttar Pradesh. In 1969, the INC expelled Gandhi from the party in a dispute over government policy and party discipline.

Gandhi and her supporters formed a new party, the INC (R), which formed India's first coalition government. In the 1971 Indian general election, the INC (R) won a landslide victory, focusing on issues such as poverty.

As prime minister, Gandhi was known for her uncompromising political stances and centralisation of power within the executive branch. In 1967, she headed a military conflict with China in which India repelled Chinese incursions into Sikkim, an Indian protectorate in the Himalayas. In the same year, the Naxalbari uprising in West Bengal was suppressed.

In 1971, she went to war with Pakistan in support of the independence movement and war of independence in East Pakistan, which resulted in an Indian victory, the end of the Bangladeshi genocide, and the independence of Bangladesh, as well as an increase in India's influence to the point where it became the sole regional power in South Asia.

The end of East Pakistan weakened the Insurgency in North-East India. In 1975, Sikkim joined the Indian Union. The same year, Kashmiri separatists had to agree to an accord establishing special autonomous status for Kashmir in return for dropping long-standing demands for a plebiscite. Jammu and Kashmir became a constituent unit of India.

Another military operation against Pakistan, codenamed Operation Meghdoot, occurred during her tenure in 1984, which led to India expanding the territory it effectively controlled in the disputed Kashmir region.

Gandhi's rule saw India grow closer to the Soviet Union by signing a friendship treaty in 1971 to ward off the perceived geopolitical threat of the alliance between the United States and Pakistan. India received military, financial, and diplomatic support from the Soviet Union during its conflict with Pakistan in the same year.

Though India was at the forefront of the Non-Aligned Movement, Gandhi made it one of the Soviet Union's closest allies in Asia, each often supporting the other at the United Nations and in proxy wars in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Afghanistan.

Gandhi played a crucial role in initiating India's first successful nuclear weapon test in 1974, codenamed 'Smiling Buddha', a year after the United States and the People's Republic of China established friendly relations, in 1973.

Responding to the verdict on State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain, and citing powers to tackle "internal disturbance" under Article 352 of the Constitution, Gandhi instituted a state of emergency from 1975 to 1977, during which she ruled by decree and basic civil liberties were suspended.

More than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned. Following the Emergency, the INC lost the 1977 Indian general election in the midst of anti-incumbency sentiment in North India, the first such loss for the INC in the history of the Republic of India.

She lost her own parliamentary constituency, Rae Bareli, albeit the INC swept the seats in South India and North-East India. She withdrew her membership of INC (R) and was publicly persecuted by the ruling Janata Party government for implementing and directing the Emergency.
However, she gained parliamentary immunity by winning the Chikmagalur by-election in Karnataka in 1978. The same year, Gandhi and her supporters formed a new political party, the INC (I).

Due to her public perception as a strong leader, public sympathy over her prosecution by the Janata Party government, and the weak governance of the Janata Party ministers, the Congress (I) won the 1980 Indian general election by a landslide and Gandhi returned to the premiership.

Gandhi faced also the Sikh separatist movement throughout her fourth premiership, in response, she ordered Operation Blue Star, which involved military action in the Golden Temple and killed hundreds of Sikhs.

On 31 October 1984, she was assassinated by two of her bodyguards, both of whom were Sikh nationalists seeking retribution for the events at the temple. Her death was the trigger for the 1984 Anti-Sikh Riots in the nation's capital, Delhi.

Her cumulative tenure of 15 years and 350 days, spanning four terms, makes her the second-longest-serving Indian prime minister after her father and the longest-serving female head of government at the time of her death.

Gandhi was cremated at the site now known as Shakti Sthal (transl. The site is marked by a large monolithic rock of iron ore commemorating her as the "Iron Lady of India". Gandhi is remembered as one of the most powerful women in the world.

Her supporters cite her leadership during victories over geopolitical rivals China and Pakistan, the Green Revolution, a growing economy in the early 1980s, and her anti-poverty campaign that led her to be known as Mother Indira among the country's poor and rural population.
Critics note her cult of personality and authoritarian rule of India during the Emergency. In 1999, she was named "Woman of the Millennium" in an online poll organised by the BBC.
In 2020, she was named by Time magazine among the 100 women who defined the past century as counterparts to the magazine's previous choices for Man of the Year.
Early life and career
Indira Gandhi was born in British ruled India as Indira Nehru, into a Kashmiri Pandit family on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad (present-day Prayagraj) in Uttar Pradesh.
Her father, Jawaharlal Nehru, was a leading figure in the Indian movement for independence from British rule, and became the first Prime Minister of the Dominion (and later Republic) of India.
Indira was her parents' only surviving child (she had a younger brother who died while young), she grew up with her mother, Kamala Nehru, at the Anand Bhavan, a large family estate in Allahabad.

In 1930, the Nehru family donated the mansion to the Indian National Congress and renamed it Swaraj Bhavan (meaning abode of freedom). A new mansion was built nearby to serve as the family residence and given the name of the old Anand Bhavan. Indira had a lonely and unhappy childhood.
